subject: Communication
title: I Have a Dream: MLK's Masterclass
description: A tiny lesson with a big payoff: I Have a Dream: MLK's Masterclass.

hook.text: On August 28, 1963, a pastor deviated from his prepared text — and changed American history.

buildup.text: Martin Luther King Jr. had typed remarks, but Mahalia Jackson shouted 'Tell them about the dream!'

discovery.text: He set aside his notes and improvised the 'I have a dream' refrain — his most iconic passage.

twist.text: The improvised section used anaphora — repeating 'I have a dream' — a technique from ancient rhetoric.

climax.text: 250,000 people heard it live. Billions have heard it since. It became the voice of a movement.

punchline.text: The greatest speech in modern history was partly unscripted.

quiz.question: What rhetorical technique did MLK use in his 'I Have a Dream' refrain?

details.summary: Martin Luther King Jr.'s 'I Have a Dream' speech is a masterclass in oratory. It combines biblical cadence, emotional crescendo, vivid imagery, and strategic repetition. Much of the most memorable section was improvised when Mahalia Jackson called out 'Tell them about the dream.'
details.whyItMatters: King's speech shows how mastery of technique enables powerful improvisation. His rhetorical skill turned a political rally into a defining moment of American history.
takeaways: Repetition of 'I have a dream' creates rhythmic power
The most famous section was partially improvised
King blended logic, emotion, and moral authority seamlessly

faq.question: What rhetorical techniques did King use in this speech?
faq.answer: Anaphora (repeating I have a dream), metaphor (the bad check of justice), allusion (biblical and constitutional references), crescendo (building emotional intensity), and call-and-response rhythm drawn from the Black church tradition. Every technique served the central message.

faq.question: How much of the speech was improvised?
faq.answer: King's prepared text did not include the I have a dream section. Gospel singer Mahalia Jackson shouted from behind him to tell them about the dream. King set aside his notes and drew on a passage he had used in previous speeches, improvising the most iconic moment.
